Physical touch can fit, but crash imagery and burnt smell together suggest a road traffic accident or fire-related trauma rather than police-related trauma, and there is no supporting memory or appraisal content tying these cues back to police trauma.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: 'Contamination/feeling dirty' is more typically coherent with sexual assault or severe bodily violation trauma. In a police-trauma profile, it is hard to reconcile this appraisal unless there are other items indicating sexualized assault, humiliating bodily violation, or related memory content, which are absent here.

A tactile trigger of general physical touch would usually imply trauma involving bodily contact/restraint. That could occur in police trauma, but in this profile there is no supporting memory or appraisal content about physical restraint, assault, or contact-based threat. Given the rest of the profile emphasizes authority/police cues, danger, mistrust, and guilt, this broad touch trigger stands out as insufficiently supported and clinically hard to place.

vignette:
Ravi was forty-one, a graphic designer in a mid-sized firm, when a routine traffic stop changed everything. He had been driving home late from a client revision, tired and distracted, when the patrol car's lights flashed behind him. The officer-a tall man in a dark uniform-approached the window and accused him of weaving. Ravi tried to explain, but his words came out tangled. The officer ordered him out, pushed him against the hood, and called for backup. From somewhere nearby, a sharp acrid smell of burnt rubber and plastic drifted across the asphalt. A car fire a block away, Ravi later learned, but in that moment the stench locked into his memory like a brand. He was released without a citation, but the officer's cold indifference-the way he looked through him as if he were nothing-left a wound that would not close.

In the weeks that followed, Ravi found himself replaying the scene at odd moments. The burnt smell from a neighbor's barbecue could send him back inside his own head, and he would feel a wave of guilt so heavy it made his chest ache-guilt that he hadn't spoken up, hadn't recorded the encounter, hadn't protected himself. Whenever he saw a police cruiser or someone in a security guard's uniform, his stomach dropped and the memory flooded back, vivid and wordless. He knew what had happened, but when his wife asked about it he could not find the words; his sentences stalled, threads lost, and he would trail off mid-explanation, ashamed. To stop those vivid, wordless replays from ambushing him during the day, Ravi began silently rehearsing every possible conversation before it happened-if he could script away the risk of being tongue-tied again, he believed, the memory might lose its power.

Because Ravi had come to believe that people in positions of authority could not be trusted-that the world was fundamentally dangerous and that he had been betrayed by someone he should have been able to rely on-his memory of the event became saturated with that betrayal. He would recall the officer's face and think, He judged me before I even spoke. This belief also made him hyperalert to any sign of threat. He started scanning crowds for uniforms, for anyone who looked like they carried authority-a crossing guard, a building security guard-and each sighting felt like a small ambush.

To manage the dread, Ravi began rehearsing conversations before any interaction. Before a meeting with his art director, he would run through possible questions and answers in his head, trying to script away the possibility of being misunderstood or humiliated. He avoided making any plans for the future-vacations, work projects more than a month out-because the thought of an unknown situation with unknown people felt unbearable. And he remained vigilant, watching for dangerous people, especially anyone in a uniformed role, even a mail carrier. These strategies gave him a momentary sense of control, but they also kept the memory close. Rehearsing reminded him of his failure to speak clearly during the stop; avoiding plans made him dwell on the helplessness he had felt. Each hypervigilant scan of a stranger's face reinforced his conviction that the world was unsafe and people could not be counted on. But the more he scanned, the more uniforms seemed to pop up wherever he looked-a delivery driver in a blue shirt, a building maintenance worker with a badge-turning ordinary people into triggers that had never bothered him before.

At work, Ravi's avoidance became visible: he stopped volunteering for new projects, declined a promotion that would require client presentations, and began taking lunch at his desk to avoid the security guard who stood near the cafeteria entrance. His boss noticed his withdrawal and pulled him aside, but Ravi simply said he was fine. He was not fine. The burnt smell from the office toaster made him flinch. The sight of a police motorcycle parked outside the building made him turn and walk the other way to a different exit. Each trigger tightened the loop: the memory, the guilt, the rehearsed silence, the avoidance, the confirmation that the world was dangerous.

What finally brought Ravi to seek help was a panic attack in the grocery store when a man in a blue uniform-a store employee-asked if he needed help. Ravi froze, his heart hammering, and he left his cart and walked out. That night, he told his wife he could not go on like this. What he feared most was losing his job, his marriage, his ability to make any kind of future. What he hoped for, barely daring to whisper it even to himself, was that he might one day walk past a uniform without feeling like he was back on that asphalt, choking on smoke.

No paragraph conveys that maladaptive strategies cause or increase triggers; the vignette describes strategies as responses to triggers, not as causing them.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Memory → Maladaptive Strategies: No paragraph conveys that the traumatic memory leads to maladaptive strategies; the vignette shows strategies are adopted to manage dread, but the causal link from memory to strategies is not explicitly stated within the same paragraph.
  e.g. "She had learned that if she kept the television on loud enough, the thoughts couldn't get a foothold — silence was the enemy."
  e.g. "After the memory surfaced during sex, she began finding quiet reasons to avoid intimacy altogether, telling herself she was simply tired or stressed."
  e.g. "To stop the images coming at night, she started staying up later and later, until exhaustion was the only reliable way to fall asleep."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers: No paragraph conveys that maladaptive strategies cause or increase triggers; the vignette describes strategies as responses to triggers, not as causing them.
  e.g. "Each place she avoided became a reminder in itself — the long way round she walked every morning was its own daily acknowledgement of what had happened."
  e.g. "Her safety behaviours had drawn a map of the event around her: everything she couldn't do, everywhere she couldn't go, every person she kept at arm's length."
  e.g. "The avoidance had grown in all directions until the city was full of routes she no longer used and things she could no longer say."
